title: Left for Dead Twice on Everest: The Full Case of Beck Weathers
description:
Case 014, the full case file. On 10 May 1996 Beck Weathers, a pathologist from Dallas, was climbing Mount Everest with an expedition led by Rob Hall. He had had eye surgery, and high on the mountain his sight failed. He stopped and waited for his leader to come back for him (accounts differ on whether he was told to wait or chose to), and he waited for most of the day. Rob Hall did not come back; he died on the mountain in the storm that followed.

Weathers started down with a group of climbers, and a blizzard caught them. They could not find the tents of the high camp, though they were close to it. During the night a rescuer brought in others from the group but not him: by one account he was judged beyond help, by another he had walked off into the storm. The next morning a doctor, Stuart Hutchison, found him still breathing and, with nothing that could be done for him there, had to leave him. Yasuko Namba, who lay beside him, did not survive. A report written at Base Camp that week says a doctor had confirmed his death, and his wife was told he was dead.

By his own count he was unconscious for about fifteen hours (other accounts say sixteen or eighteen). That afternoon he woke with his right hand bare and frozen solid, stood up and walked into camp. He was put in a tent and not expected to live through the night, and did. He was helped down on foot to a lower camp, and an army pilot, Lt. Col. Madan K.C., flew one of the highest helicopter rescues made up to that time, setting down above the icefall (about 20,000 feet, by one report from that week) to lift two climbers off the mountain. He lost his right hand and part of the forearm, the fingers of his left hand, parts of both feet and his nose, which surgeons rebuilt. He went home to his family and wrote a book, Left for Dead. Rob Hall, Yasuko Namba and other climbers died in that storm. Rook didn't believe it either.

Animated reconstruction of a true story. The mountain, camps, tents, radio tent, ice face, helicopter and its cabin, hospital room, study and house in the film are generic low-poly sets, not models of the real places or aircraft; the other people (the leader, the climbers, the radio operator, the pilot) are anonymous stand-ins, not likenesses; Yasuko Namba is not depicted. The cards, the report sheet, the mountain diagram and the book cover are drawings made for the film, not real documents, maps or covers. Where sources disagree the film says so.
source_notes: Seven pages were read for this run on 15 Nov 2026 (the first attempt was refused, the second went through): Wikipedia 'Beck Weathers' (WP-BW, in full); Wikipedia '1996 Mount Everest disaster' (WP-96, the first half word for word, the rest only as a summary, which is not relied on); PBS NOVA Online, Audrey Salkeld's report from Base Camp dated 16 May 1996 (NOVA, in full); The Washington Post live discussion with Beck Weathers, 11 May 2000 (WaPo, in full); The Irish Times, 'Rebirth on the summit', 1 July 2000 (IT, in full); PBS Frontline, 'Storm Over Everest: the unfolding disaster' (FL, word for word up to the morning of 11 May; later parts only as a summary, not relied on); All That's Interesting, 2021/2024 (ATI, in full). Britannica could not be fetched and HowStuffWorks returned an empty page, so nothing rests on them. Narrated facts and where they are: 10 May 1996 (WaPo, WP-96). Pathologist (WP-BW, IT, ATI) from Dallas (WP-BW, WaPo, IT). Expedition led by Rob Hall (WP-BW, IT, ATI, FL). Eye surgery and failing sight at altitude (WP-BW and ATI: radial keratotomy; FL: 'aftereffects of eye surgery'; NOVA: 'difficulty seeing'). Told to wait or chose to: ATI says Hall ordered him, WP-BW that Hall advised it, FL that he told Hall he would sit and wait; narrated as 'accounts differ'. Waited most of the day (FL: from sunrise to dusk; ATI: almost ten hours). Hall did not come back and died on the mountain (WP-BW, WP-96, ATI). Started down with other climbers and the blizzard hit; they could not find the high camp though close to it (WP-BW 'could not find Camp IV'; WP-96: the camp was some 400 m away when the storm cleared; FL; IT). The night: ATI says a guide rescued others and 'deemed Weathers beyond help', IT that he and Namba were 'left to die'; WP-BW and WP-96 say he had stood up and disappeared into the storm when the rescuer came. The narration gives both ('by one account ... by another'). Next morning Stuart Hutchison went out, found him alive and left him (WP-BW, IT; ATI 'a Canadian doctor' found him 'still breathing'; FL heading). Yasuko Namba lay beside him and died (WP-BW, WP-96, NOVA, IT); she is named and not shown. 'His death had been confirmed by a doctor': NOVA's report, in those words; this is the one page that says it and the narration attributes it to 'a report written at Base Camp that week'. His wife was told he was dead (IT, ATI). About fifteen hours unconscious by his own count (WaPo, his words; IT), sixteen (NOVA), eighteen (WaPo introduction). Woke that afternoon (ATI about 4 p.m.; NOVA), right hand bare and frozen solid (IT 'gloveless and frozen rock-solid'; ATI; FL has the lost glove). The vision of his family: IT only (a feature on his book); in the WaPo discussion he says he does not know what made him open his eyes, so it is narrated as 'by one telling of his story' and labelled the same way on screen. Stood up and walked into camp under his own power (WP-BW, WP-96, IT, ATI, NOVA). Put in a tent, made comfortable, expected to die, alive in the morning (WP-BW, IT, WP-96; ATI alone says he spent that night in the open, which the film does not follow). Hands and arms 'frozen to the elbows': NOVA only, narrated as 'by one report'. Helped down on foot to a lower camp (WP-BW, WP-96, NOVA, ATI). Helicopter: 'one of the highest aerial rescues ever' (NOVA), 'one of the highest ever attempted' (WP-96), 'the highest-altitude medical evacuation ever performed by helicopter up until that time' (WP-BW); pilot Lt. Colonel Madan K.C. in an army helicopter (NOVA; IT gives his full name); above the Icefall at 20,000 ft (NOVA only for the figure, narrated as 'one report from that week'); two climbers flown out, the other being Makalu Gau (NOVA, WP-96; IT two trips). The Irish Times calls the pilot Taiwanese, which no other page read supports; no nationality is stated in the film. Injuries: right hand and part of the forearm, the fingers of the left hand (WP-BW, WP-96, ATI; WP-BW adds the left thumb, IT says half of it remains, so the thumb is not mentioned and the drawn left hand keeps it), parts of both feet (WP-BW, ATI), nose rebuilt (WP-BW, IT, ATI). Home to his family (WaPo, IT) and the book Left for Dead (WP-BW, WaPo, ATI). Other climbers died in the storm: the pages give eight (WP-96, IT) or nine (WaPo, ATI), so no number is stated. Left out because the pages disagree or only one has it: the altitude and name of the place where he waited, the distance to the tents, whether his tent collapsed in the night, who exactly helped him down, the aircraft type, how the nose was rebuilt, and his wife's part in arranging the rescue. Rook's lines about himself (his hat, his record, 'I wouldn't have bet on any of them') are the host's comments, not facts about the case.

sound_plan: Wind and one boom on the first frame; score follows the script moods (hook, tense, action, sad for the night, the morning, Namba and the telephone call, wonder for the waking, triumph for the walk and the helicopter, calm for the cost, sad for the memorial, end). Every shot has at least one story sound (wind, ticks, heartbeat, rotor).
